nameStory: The 'pitseed' part of this plant's name comes from its most distinctive feature - seeds that look like tiny honeycombs, covered in small pits or depressions. 'Goosefoot' refers to the shape of the leaves, which reminded early botanists of a goose's webbed foot. This humble plant has quite a resume, having fed Native American communities for thousands of years before being largely forgotten as a food crop.
description: Pitseed goosefoot is a fast-growing annual plant that can shoot up to 10 feet tall in a single growing season, though most stay around 3-6 feet. It has an upright, branching structure with diamond-shaped leaves that have wavy, toothed edges - especially on the lower part of the plant. The tiny greenish flowers cluster together in dense, branched spikes, and the whole plant has a somewhat dusty or mealy appearance, especially on the undersides of young leaves.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: The seeds are the plant's calling card - small, dark, and covered in tiny pits that create a honeycomb pattern when viewed closely. Feel one between your fingers and you'll notice it's quite hard and smooth despite the textured surface.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are distinctly diamond-shaped with evenly spaced, sharp teeth along the edges, while upper leaves become narrower and less toothed. Young leaves feel slightly mealy or dusty underneath, almost like they've been dusted with flour.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish flowers without petals cluster in dense, branching spikes at the stem tips and leaf joints. The flower clusters feel rough and papery when mature, and often have a slightly dusty appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a single-stemmed annual that branches extensively, creating a somewhat pyramid-shaped plant. The main stem feels sturdy and slightly ridged, often developing reddish streaks as it matures.

idTips.label: Overall Texture
idTips.description: The whole plant has a distinctive mealy or dusty quality, especially noticeable when you brush against it or rub the leaves gently. This powdery coating can sometimes rub off on your fingers.

habitat: Look for pitseed goosefoot in disturbed soils like gardens, farm edges, vacant lots, and roadsides throughout New England. It thrives in rich, well-drained soils and full sun, often popping up wherever the ground has been recently turned or disturbed. You'll frequently find it growing alongside other weedy plants like common lambsquarters and pigweed in agricultural areas.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge in late spring as small rosettes with distinctly diamond-shaped, toothed leaves that feel mealy underneath. Look for the characteristic dusty coating on new growth.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly and begin flowering in mid to late summer, producing the distinctive branched clusters of tiny green flowers. This is when the plant reaches its full impressive height.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature in early fall, developing their characteristic honeycomb-pitted surface. The whole plant begins to turn yellow and brown, but the seed heads persist and rattle when shaken.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist into winter, with dried seed heads still attached. The distinctive pitted seeds can often be found scattered on the ground beneath where plants grew.

funFact: This 'weed' was actually one of the first crops domesticated in North America - Native Americans were cultivating it for food over 4,000 years ago, centuries before corn arrived from Mexico, and they developed varieties with seeds twice the size of wild plants!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common lambsquarters, but pitseed goosefoot's lower leaves have much more pronounced, evenly-spaced teeth (lambsquarters' leaves are more wavy than truly toothed). Memory trick: 'Pitseed has pointed teeth' - both start with 'p' and refer to the distinctive serrated lower leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite sharing the common name 'lamb's quarters' with its close relative Chenopodium album, pitseed goosefoot is a distinct species that was independently domesticated in eastern North America. In Mexico, it's still cultivated today under the name 'huauzontle' and eaten like broccoli, showing how cultural knowledge can preserve what others might dismiss as just a weed.
compareHints: Among New England goosefoots, pitseed goosefoot stands out for its strongly toothed lower leaves and honeycomb-pitted seeds. Common lambsquarters has more wavy-edged leaves and smooth seeds, while other goosefoots in the region tend to be much smaller plants or have different leaf shapes entirely. The combination of size, leaf teeth, and pitted seeds makes this species quite distinctive once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common lambsquarters is much more widespread than its relatives like pitseed goosefoot or fig-leaved goosefoot in New England.
Fogg's goosefoot is distinguished from Common Lambsquarters by having more triangular, less elongated leaves and typically being smaller overall.
Unlike common lambsquarters which has simple diamond or triangular leaves, fig-leaved goosefoot has deeply divided, lobed leaves that are unmistakable.

Desert goosefoot stands out from other New England goosefoots primarily by its exceptionally powdery texture - much more pronounced than the light dustiness of common lambsquarters or other relatives.
Tree spinach dwarfs its goosefoot relatives like common lambsquarters, which rarely exceed 3-4 feet tall and have much thinner stems.
Unlike the common lambsquarters with its plain green leaves dusted with white powder, striped goosefoot has those unmistakable light stripes running through each leaf.
